title: Noah builds (Genesis 6:5–22)
hookLine: in a violent world, one man builds a boat on dry land

lines: THE WORLD GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE.
ONE MAN, A SET OF PLANS.
cards: Somewhere right now, someone is working on a thing nobody around them believes in. A novel in a drawer. A garden in a vacant lot.
A recovery, ninety days in. Friends ask, gently, how long you're going to keep at that. In Genesis, the world after the garden goes from bad to worse.
One murder becomes many. And in the middle of it, one man is handed a set of building plans for something enormous, for a disaster nobody can see coming.

teach.b: Chapter six opens with grief. God sees that the wickedness of humans is great, and the text says it grieved him at his heart. Then the diagnosis, in the King James Bible: "the earth was filled with violence."
The Hebrew word for violence there is chamas: brutality, wrong done to others.

But one verse cuts across the darkness: "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." Noah, the text says, was a just man, and he walked with God, the same phrase used for Enoch yesterday. So God gives him plans.
An ark of gopher wood, nobody's quite sure what tree that is, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high. A building, lying on its side.

teach.h: TEVAH: A BOX, LIKE MOSES'S BASKET.
teach.b: And the Hebrew word for ark, tevah, isn't the usual word for a ship. It means something like a box, a chest. The same word turns up again in Exodus, for the little basket of reeds that carries baby Moses on the Nile.
Two boxes, one huge and one tiny, each carrying the future through deadly water. Popular retellings add crowds of neighbors mocking him. Genesis doesn't.
A later New Testament letter calls Noah a preacher of righteousness, but the chapter itself gives him no lines at all. Noah never says a word until after the flood.
What it records is this: "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he."
That's the week's last step: from a person alone, a twisting question, a call to come out, clothes for the road, a brother to keep, a slow walk, to a man who just builds.

how: Christians often see Noah as a model of faithful obedience, and early Christian writers used the ark as a picture of the church and of baptism, carrying people safely through the water.

games.q: you're Noah. God has handed you plans for a box of wood the length of a building lying on its side, for a flood nobody can see. what does the text say you do?
o: argue with God about the size.
everything God commanded, without a word.
games.why: "thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he." in Genesis, Noah says nothing until after the flood.

practice: Think of something you're building that not everyone believes in, a habit, a project, a relationship, and picture it as it is: half-finished, a frame of boards on dry land, with the doubts around it.
Then picture just the next plank, one small thing. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Ark. Tevah in Hebrew, a box or chest. The huge boat Noah builds, and the same word as the tiny basket that carries baby Moses.
